questions.q: What is the defining property of a well-built modular monolith?
options: Each internal module is deployed on its own dedicated server for isolation
One deployable unit with internal module boundaries enforced in code
A single process that deliberately forbids any internal code boundaries
Multiple databases, one per module, joined together at query time

questions.q: What is the primary organizational benefit claimed for microservices?
options: Every team writes in one mandated language, which eases hiring
There are fewer repositories to maintain across the organization
Teams can deploy and scale their services independently
All services share one database schema, which eases joins

questions.q: What immediate cost appears when an in-process call becomes a network hop?
options: It can fail, time out, or be slow, and needs retries and monitoring
It must be rewritten in a compiled language to stay fast enough
It requires a message broker placed between every pair of services
It doubles the number of database connections each service holds

questions.q: Why do microservices typically avoid sharing one database?
options: Databases cannot accept connections from more than one service
Shared databases are inherently slower than dedicated per-service databases by design
Database licensing usually charges per connecting application
Shared schemas couple services, so one team's change breaks others

questions.q: In a monolith, how do modules typically communicate?
options: Through HTTP calls routed via the operating system's loopback
Through a shared message broker embedded inside the process
Through in-process function calls, cheap and transactional
Through files written into a shared temporary directory

questions.q: Which deployment property do monoliths retain that microservices lose?
options: The ability to roll back any component without redeploying anything else
Atomic releases: all code ships together at one consistent version
Zero-downtime deploys via rolling replacement of instances
The ability to canary a release to a small fraction of traffic

questions.q: Which scenario genuinely favors extracting a module into its own service?
options: A module whose formatting and code style differ noticeably from the rest of the codebase
A module whose unit tests run slower than the others in CI
A module maintained by the same team as all of its callers
A module with resource needs wildly different from the rest, like GPU inference

questions.q: What is a distributed monolith?
options: Services so entangled they must be deployed and changed together
A monolith replicated across regions behind a global balancer
A monolith whose modules run in separate operating system threads
Any system mixing REST calls with message-based communication

questions.q: Checkout spans orders, payments, and inventory services. What replaces the monolith's single ACID transaction?
options: A distributed lock held across all three services during checkout
Two-phase commit coordinated by the API gateway on every request
Eventual consistency achieved by retrying the whole checkout nightly
A saga: local transactions with compensating actions on failure

questions.q: A startup has 6 engineers and unclear domain boundaries. Why start with a monolith?
options: Boundaries are still shifting; refactoring in-process is far cheaper than redrawing service contracts
Monolithic architectures handle strictly more traffic than microservices at every conceivable scale
Microservices cannot be built by engineering teams smaller than ten people
Investors and auditors generally require a single deployable artifact

questions.q: A shared library of domain models is used by 15 services. What is the hidden danger?
options: Library code runs measurably slower than service-local code due to linking
Every model change forces coordinated upgrades, re-coupling the services
Shared libraries cannot be versioned in modern package managers
It prevents the services from ever being written in the same language

questions.q: A page now fans out to 8 sequential service calls of ~25ms each; the monolith took 30ms total. What is the lesson?
options: Network fan-out is free once HTTP/2 multiplexing has been enabled
The services simply need a faster serialization format, which will restore the original 30ms
In-process calls became network hops; latency adds up and needs parallelism or aggregation
Latency is unrelated to architecture and comes entirely from the database

questions.q: Debugging a failed request now spans six services. What tooling becomes essential?
options: Distributed tracing with correlation IDs propagated across calls
A shared debugger attached to all six processes at once
Verbose logging enabled permanently at debug level everywhere
A scheduled job that diffs each service's database nightly

questions.q: Traffic doubles, the team is 5 people, and the bottleneck is one SQL query. Why avoid splitting into services?
options: Because microservices cannot run on ordinary cloud virtual machines
Because service extraction always requires a full rewrite of the data layer
The bottleneck is a query; splitting adds operational load without fixing it
Because the database cannot be accessed by two services at once

questions.q: What does Conway's law imply for choosing service boundaries?
options: Service boundaries should precisely follow the foreign keys between database tables
Each service should be small enough for one engineer to rewrite in two weeks
Boundaries should be drawn to minimize the total number of services
Architecture mirrors team communication, so align services with team ownership

questions.q: What is the recommended pattern for safely extracting the first service from a monolith?
options: Big-bang rewrite: freeze the monolith and rebuild everything as services
Strangler fig: route traffic incrementally to the new service behind a facade
Fork the monolith into two full copies and split the traffic by user ID
Extract the database first, then move the application code six months later

questions.q: An org runs 40 services with 5 engineers; delivery is slow and the pager never stops. What is the root issue?
options: Too few services; finer granularity would isolate the failures better
A missing service mesh; sidecar proxies would eliminate the operational toil
Service count wildly exceeds team capacity; operational overhead dominates feature work
Wrong language choices; consolidating onto one runtime fixes the pager load

questions.q: A service writes its database then publishes an event, and can crash in between. What is the robust fix?
options: Wrap the database write and the broker publish inside one XA transaction spanning both systems
Publish the event first, then perform the database write inside the event handler
Add a retry loop around the publish until it succeeds at least once
Transactional outbox: write the event to the DB atomically, relay it asynchronously

questions.q: A monolith ran at 60% CPU on 20 VMs. Split into 8 services with the same traffic, total footprint grows. Why?
options: Per-service overhead (runtimes, sidecars, headroom) and serialization costs multiply across services
Cloud providers charge a per-service premium on otherwise identical VMs
Microservices require synchronous replication of every incoming request
Every mainstream orchestrator reserves one full virtual machine per service by default

questions.q: A flow degrades when any of 5 chained services is slow; each meets a 99.9% SLO. What is the effect and lever?
options: Availability multiplies out to 99.9% overall, so no action is needed beyond monitoring
Tail latencies compound across the chain; cut serial depth, add hedging or caching
Only the slowest single service matters; tune that one and every SLO is met
The gateway absorbs the slowness, so SLOs only apply to edge services
